Your task is to generate a complete research paper using the materials below.
You must produce:
1. A BibTeX bibliography file (references.bib)
2. The full LaTeX paper (template.tex)

Instructions
• Use the research idea and experimental logs to construct a coherent, rigorous ML paper.
• For related work and baselines:
  – Search for and include influential papers published up until 2024-10.
  – Incorporate relevant literature and add the corresponding BibTeX entries to references.bib.
  – Do NOT hallucinate papers or reference keys; all citation entries must be real.
• In the LaTeX paper, cite papers using \cite{} with keys that match exactly with your entries in references.bib.
• Do not fabricate experimental results or make claims unsupported by the logs.

Materials
Here are all the raw research materials to assist with the writing process:

[RESEARCH IDEA]
## Problem Statement
Autoregressive (AR) models currently set the state-of-the-art for image and text generation, but they suffer from a significant computational bottleneck: they must generate data sequentially, token-by-token. Existing attempts to accelerate this process (e.g., parallel decoding) fail to capture the true joint distribution of the output. When these methods attempt to generate multiple tokens simultaneously, they essentially assume conditional independence between tokens or attempt to learn a one-to-many mapping from a prefix to multiple future possibilities. This inevitably leads to mode collapse or "blurry," averaged outputs, making high-quality, few-step (or one-step) AR generation effectively impossible with current techniques.

## Core Hypothesis
We hypothesize that the fundamental limitation of parallel AR generation—the one-to-many mapping problem—can be resolved by artificially constructing a **deterministic** mapping from a prior noise distribution to the AR model's output distribution.

By integrating **Flow Matching (FM)** into the AR decoding process, we can transform the probabilistic sampling of the teacher model into a deterministic Ordinary Differential Equation (ODE) trajectory. We believe that if we distill this specific deterministic trajectory into a student model, we can enable a pre-trained AR model to generate an entire sequence of tokens in a single step (or very few steps) without requiring the original training data.

## Proposed Methodology (High-Level Technical Approach)
We propose a "Distilled Decoding" framework that bridges autoregressive modeling with continuous flow matching. The approach consists of two distinct phases: Trajectory Construction (Data Generation) and Student Distillation.

**1. Deterministic Trajectory Construction via Flow Matching**
Instead of using standard sampling techniques (which are stochastic), we will use the pre-trained AR "teacher" model to define a velocity field. For every step in the sequence, we will employ Flow Matching to map a random Gaussian noise token to the target token embedding predicted by the AR model.
*   We will solve the flow ODE to create a continuous path from a sequence of pure noise tokens to a sequence of valid data tokens.
*   Crucially, this process creates a strict **one-to-one mapping** between the initial noise sequence and the final generated content. This eliminates the multimodal uncertainty that plagues standard parallel decoding.

**2. Trajectory Distillation**
Once we have generated a dataset of these synthetic (Noise Sequence $\rightarrow$ Data Sequence) pairs using the teacher, we will train a student model to learn this mapping directly.
*   **Architecture:** The student will mirror the teacher's architecture but will be modified to accept an entire sequence of noise embeddings as input.
*   **Training Objective:** The student will be trained to regress the final data sequence given the starting noise sequence (or an intermediate point in the flow trajectory).
*   **Flexible Inference:** By training on various points along the trajectory, the system will allow for a trade-off between speed and quality. We can perform 1-step generation (predicting the end directly from noise) or few-step generation (predicting intermediate states to refine quality), and we can even interleave the original AR model for specific segments if higher precision is required.

## Expected Contribution
*   **Theoretical Novelty:** We aim to challenge the prevailing assumption that AR models must be inherently sequential, demonstrating that they can be adapted for 1-step generation through deterministic flow mappings.
*   **Practical Efficiency:** This approach offers orders-of-magnitude speedups for AR inference, converting $N$-step processes into 1 or 2 steps.
*   **Data Independence:** Unlike many distillation methods, our proposal generates its own training pairings via the teacher model, eliminating the need for access to the teacher's original, potentially proprietary, training dataset.

[EXPERIMENTAL LOGS]
## 1. Experimental Setup

We evaluated the proposed Distilled Decoding (DD) method primarily on image generation tasks, with an additional evaluation on text-to-image generation.

*   **Datasets:**
    *   **ImageNet-256:** Used for class-conditional image generation. We generated 1.2 million data-noise pairs for the distillation process.
    *   **LAION-COCO:** Used for text-to-image generation tasks. We generated 3 million data-noise pairs. For evaluation, we generated images based on 5,000 unseen prompts from this dataset.

*   **Teacher Models (Pre-trained AR Models):**
    *   **VAR:** Visual Autoregressive modeling (scales: d16, d20, d24). Uses multi-scale token prediction (10 steps for 256x256 images).
    *   **LlamaGen:** A standard raster-order autoregressive model (scales: L, B). Uses 256 steps for 256x256 images.

*   **Baselines Compared:**
    *   **Original Teacher Models:** VAR (d16, d20, d24) and LlamaGen (L, B).
    *   **Skip-step Baselines:** "skip-n" (skipping the last n steps of the AR model).
    *   **One-step Baseline:** "onestep*" (predicting the distribution of all tokens in one step based on dataset token frequency).
    *   **External Methods (for reference):** GANs (StyleGAN-XL), Diffusion Models (ADM, LDM-4-G, DiT-L/2, L-DiT-7B), Masked Generative Models (MaskGIT), and older AR models (VQVAE-2, VQGAN, ViTVQ, RQTransformer).

*   **Evaluation Metrics:**
    *   **FID:** Fréchet Inception Distance (Lower is better).
    *   **IS:** Inception Score (Higher is better).
    *   **Pre:** Precision (Higher is better).
    *   **Rec:** Recall (Higher is better).
    *   **Time:** Wall-time for generating one image in steady state (measured in seconds).
    *   **Speedup:** Relative speed increase compared to the teacher model.

*   **Implementation Details:**
    *   **Distillation Training:**
        *   **VAR Distillation:** Trained for 120 epochs, batch size 512, base learning rate 1e-4 per 256 batch size.
        *   **LlamaGen Distillation:** Trained for 70 epochs, fixed learning rate 1e-4.
    *   **Optimizer:** AdamW with $\beta_1=0.9, \beta_2=0.95$.
    *   **Loss:** Weighted sum of Cross Entropy (logit prediction, weight 0.1) and LPIPS (embedding prediction, weight 1.0).
    *   **Data Generation:** Classifier-free guidance scale set to 2.0. Used DPM-Solver++ (10 NFE) for flow matching trajectory construction.
    *   **Sampling:** Used Alg. 3 (Standard DD) and Alg. 4 (DD + Pre-trained AR hybrid) for inference.

## 3. Qualitative Observations

*   **Comparison to Baselines:**
    *   We observed that the naive "skip" baselines (simply reducing steps in the original model) resulted in rapid performance degradation as the number of skipped steps increased.
    *   The "onestep*" baseline (predicting token distribution based on dataset statistics) failed completely, resulting in FID scores greater than 100 for both VAR and LlamaGen.
    *   Observation: Existing parallel decoding methods cannot match the generated distribution of the original AR model in a one-step setting due to conditional dependencies between tokens.

*   **Speed vs. Quality Trade-off:**
    *   We observed that DD reduced generation steps for VAR from 10 to 1, achieving a 6.3x speedup with an FID increase from 4.19 to 9.94.
    *   For LlamaGen, DD reduced steps from 256 to 1, achieving a 217.8x speedup with an FID increase from 4.11 to 11.35.
    *   Increasing DD generation to 2 steps consistently improved FID (e.g., LlamaGen-DD improved from 11.35 to 7.58) while maintaining high speedups (>100x).
    *   In the text-to-image task, the 2-step DD model achieved an FID of 28.95, comparable to the teacher's 25.70, but with a 92.9x speedup.

*   **Hybrid Generation (DD + Pre-trained AR):**
    *   We found that utilizing the pre-trained AR model to re-generate specific intermediate tokens in a DD-generated sequence provided a flexible trade-off.
    *   For VAR, replacing the first step partially with the pre-trained model yielded an FID of 5.03 (very close to the teacher's 4.19) while still being 1.5x faster.
    *   For LlamaGen, this hybrid approach achieved an FID of 6.76 with an 11.2x speedup.

*   **Scalability:**
    *   We observed that DD scaled effectively across model sizes. Larger teacher models (e.g., VAR-d24 vs VAR-d20) resulted in better performing DD students.
    *   Observation: DD works across different token sequence definitions (multi-scale for VAR, raster order for LlamaGen).

*   **Ablation Observations:**
    *   **Training Iterations:** Few-step FID decreased rapidly in the first few epochs, suggesting high adaptability of the pre-trained AR model for this task.
    *   **Intermediate Timesteps:** We observed that the method was not sensitive to the choice of intermediate timesteps during distillation; convergence speed and performance were similar across choices.
    *   **Dataset Size:** DD remained functional with as few as 0.6M data-noise pairs, though performance improved with larger dataset sizes (up to 1.6M tested).

*   **Visual Quality:**
    *   Qualitative samples showed that DD-generated images maintained semantic coherence and sharpness comparable to the teacher model, whereas baseline outputs at low step counts exhibited severe degradation or noise.

Conference Guidelines
# ICLR 2025 Paper Writing Guidelines

Below are the instructions to help you with the LaTeX paper writing process for ICLR 2025.

## General Setup
* **Document Class:** `\documentclass{article}`
* **Required Packages:**
    ```latex
    \usepackage{iclr2025_conference,times}
    \usepackage{hyperref}
    \usepackage{url}
    % Optional but recommended for math
    \input{math_commands.tex}
    ```
* **Style Files:** You must use `iclr2025_conference.sty` and `iclr2025_conference.bst`.

## Anonymity (Crucial)
* ICLR is double-blind. **Do not** include real author names or affiliations in the submission version, use "Ambitious AI Researcher" instead.
* Use the third person when citing your own prior work (e.g., "Earlier work by Smalle (2024)..." instead of "In our earlier work...").
* You may post your paper on arXiv, but do not explicitly refer to the arXiv version in the paper to maintain anonymity.

## Paper Length
* **Main Text:** Strict upper limit of **10 pages**.
* **Citations:** Unlimited additional pages.
* **Ethics & Reproducibility Statements:** Optional. Do not count toward the page limit (max 1 page each).
* **Acknowledgments:** Do not count toward the page limit.

## Abstract
The abstract must be limited to **one paragraph**.
* **Margins:** Indented 1/2 inch (3 picas) on both left and right-hand margins.
* **Font:** 10-point type, vertical spacing of 11-points.
* **Title:** The word `\textsc{Abstract}` must be centered, in small caps, and in point size 12.
* **Spacing:** Two line spaces precede the abstract.

## Formatting Your Paper
The text must be confined within a rectangle 5.5 inches (33 picas) wide and 9 inches (54 picas) long. The left margin is 1.5 inch (9 picas).
* **Font:** Times New Roman (via `times` package) is preferred.
* **Size:** 10-point type with 11-point vertical spacing.
* **Paragraphs:** Separated by 1/2 line space, with **no indentation**.
* **Paper Title:** 17-point, small caps, left-aligned.

### Headings
* **First Level:** Small caps (`\textsc`), flush left, 12-point. One line space before, 1/2 after.
* **Second Level:** Small caps, flush left, 10-point. One line space before, 1/2 after.
* **Third Level:** Small caps, flush left, 10-point. One line space before, 1/2 after.

## Citations and References
Use the `natbib` package (loaded automatically by the style file).
* **Narrative citation:** Use `\citet{Gomu2024}` $\rightarrow$ "Gomu et al. (2024)".
* **Parenthetical citation:** Use `\citep{Gomu2024}` $\rightarrow$ "(Gomu et al., 2024)".
* **Bibliography:**
    ```latex
    \bibliography{references}
    \bibliographystyle{iclr2025_conference}
    ```

## Figures and Tables
* All artwork must be neat, clean, and legible.
* **Captions:** Lower case (except for first word and proper nouns).
* **Placement:**
    * **Figures:** Caption appears **after** (below) the figure.
    * **Tables:** Caption appears **before** (above) the table.

references.text:
## Problem Statement
Autoregressive (AR) models are currently the state-of-the-art for image and text generation, yet they suffer from a severe computational bottleneck: the sequential, token-by-token generation process. To generate a sequence of length $n$, an AR model requires $n$ forward passes. While parallel decoding strategies (generating multiple tokens simultaneously) have been proposed, they fundamentally fail to capture the true joint distribution of the data.

Specifically, we identify that parallel sampling assumes conditional independence among tokens given a prefix, which is theoretically incorrect for correlated data like images. Furthermore, attempting to train a network to output all subsequent tokens in a single step (without a deterministic mapping) leads to a one-to-many mapping problem. In such scenarios, the network minimizes error by averaging all possible modes, resulting in blurry or incoherent outputs. We aim to solve the problem of adapting pre-trained AR models to generate high-fidelity outputs in as few as one or two steps, without retraining on the original dataset or sacrificing the conditional dependency inherent in the data.

## Core Hypothesis
We propose **Distilled Decoding (DD)**. Our core hypothesis is that while the mapping from a sequence of noise to a sequence of data is stochastic and multi-modal in standard AR sampling, we can construct a **deterministic probability path** from a Gaussian distribution to the AR model’s output distribution using Flow Matching (FM).

By utilizing the pre-trained AR model to define the vector field for Flow Matching, we can mathematically guarantee that the distribution of tokens generated via this path matches the AR model's conditional distribution. Once this deterministic trajectory is established, we can train a student network to distill this entire trajectory into a single step (or very few steps). We hypothesize that this approach will allow for $O(1)$ generation complexity while maintaining the high fidelity of the original $O(n)$ AR teacher.

## Proposed Methodology (Detailed Technical Approach)

We will develop a framework that synergizes Autoregressive modeling with Flow Matching to enable one-step sampling.

### 1. Constructing Deterministic Trajectories via Flow Matching
We cannot directly train a model to predict $p(q_{k+1}, \dots, q_n | q_{1}, \dots, q_k)$ in one shot due to multimodal collapse. Instead, we will construct a one-to-one deterministic mapping.

**Single Token Mapping:**
Consider the generation of a single token $q_i$ given a prefix $q_{<i}$. The AR model provides a conditional discrete distribution over the codebook $\mathcal{V} = \{c_1, \dots, c_V\}$:
$$ \mathbb{P}(q_i = c_j) = p_j, \quad \text{where } \sum p_j = 1 $$
We will view this as a mixture of Dirac delta distributions in the continuous embedding space: $p(q_i) = \sum_{j=1}^V p_j \delta(q_i - c_j)$.
We will use Flow Matching to map a standard Gaussian noise token $\epsilon_i \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I)$ to this distribution. We define the velocity field $V(x, t)$ at timestep $t \in [0, 1]$ using a linear interpolation perturb function $\varphi(x_0, x_1, t) = (1-t)x_0 + tx_1$:

$$ V(x, t) = \frac{\sum_{j=1}^V p_j (c_j - x) e^{\frac{(x - t c_j)^2}{(1-t)^2}}}{(1-t) \sum_{j=1}^V p_j e^{\frac{(x - t c_j)^2}{(1-t)^2}}} $$

By solving the ODE $dx = V(x,t)dt$, we define a deterministic mapping function:
$$ q_i = FM(\epsilon_i, p_\theta(\cdot | q_{<i})) $$

**Whole Sequence Trajectory:**
We will extend this iteratively to construct a trajectory for the entire sequence. Starting with a pure noise sequence $X_1 = (\epsilon_1, \dots, \epsilon_n)$, we generate the first token $q_1$ from $\epsilon_1$, then update the sequence to generate $q_2$ from $\epsilon_2$ conditioned on $q_1$, and so on. This defines a trajectory of intermediate sequences $\{X_i\}_{i=1}^{n+1}$ where:
$$ X_i = (q_1, \dots, q_{i-1}, \epsilon_i, \dots, \epsilon_n) $$
This trajectory smoothly transforms pure noise into the final data sequence determined by the teacher AR model.

### 2. Distillation Formulation
We will train a student model $f_\theta$ to predict the final data sequence $X_{n+1}$ from an intermediate point $X_t$ in the trajectory.

**Model Parameterization:**
The model takes an intermediate sequence $X_t$ (containing $t-1$ solved tokens and $n-t+1$ noise tokens) and the position index $t$ as input. The output prediction $F_\theta(X_t, t)$ is parameterized as:
$$ F_\theta(X_t, t) = \text{Concat}(X_t[:t-1], f_\theta(X_t)[t:]) $$
This explicitly retains the already generated tokens $q_{<t}$.

**Training Objective:**
We will minimize the distance between the student's prediction and the ground-truth final sequence $X_{n+1}$ generated by the teacher's trajectory. The loss function $\mathcal{L}$ is defined as:
$$ \mathcal{L} = \mathbb{E}_{t, X_1} [\lambda(t) d(F_\theta(X_t, t), X_{n+1})] $$
where:
*   $t$ is sampled uniformly from available timesteps.
*   $X_1 \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I)$.
*   $X_{n+1}$ is the target data derived from $X_1$ using the trajectory construction described above.
*   $d(\cdot, \cdot)$ is a distance metric.

### 3. Architecture and Loss Implementation
The student model will inherit the architecture of the pre-trained AR teacher (e.g., Transformer backbone) to facilitate convergence, with specific modifications:
1.  **Input Embeddings:** We will introduce distinct learnable embeddings for "noise tokens" and "data tokens" to allow the network to distinguish between solved prefix tokens and future noise tokens.
2.  **Position Embedding:** We will extend the positional embedding length by 1 to accommodate the full noise sequence relative to the class token.
3.  **Dual Prediction Heads:** The model will solve both a classification task and a regression task.
    *   **Logits Head:** Outputs $p \in \mathbb{R}^V$ (predicted logits). Loss: Cross Entropy.
    *   **Embedding Head:** Outputs $c \in \mathbb{R}^C$ (predicted latent vector). Loss: LPIPS (perceptual loss).
    *   We will use a weighted sum of these losses. We anticipate using logits for early-stage tokens and embeddings for later-stage tokens during inference.

### 4. Sampling Strategy
During inference, we can flexibly choose the number of steps. For one-step generation, we input pure noise $X_1$ and ask the model to predict $X_{n+1}$. For multi-step generation (e.g., 2 steps), we will predict an intermediate state $X_k$, replacing the later tokens with noise, and then predict $X_{n+1}$ from $X_k$. This allows a trade-off between inference latency and generation quality.

## Expected Contribution
1.  **Theoretical Advancement:** We aim to refute the assumption that AR generation must be sequential. We will provide the first theoretical framework combining Flow Matching and AR to create deterministic, distillable trajectories for discrete sequences.
2.  **Efficiency:** We expect to achieve order-of-magnitude speedups (e.g., reducing 256 steps to 1) for state-of-the-art Image AR models.
3.  **Data-Free Distillation:** A critical practical contribution is that our method requires *only* the pre-trained teacher model, not the original massive training dataset, making it deployable on closed-source models where data is inaccessible.
4.  **Flexible Inference:** The proposed method will allow dynamic trade-offs between image quality and latency by varying the number of decoding steps at runtime without retraining.

notes.second_provider: No OPENAI/GEMINI key is supplied (concept figures stay in deterministic export mode).

preinstalled.en: python:3.11 bookworm; upstream code via PYTHONPATH; pdflatex + bibtex; CPU PyTorch with numpy, scipy, scikit-learn, pandas, matplotlib and more (pinned by constraints.txt)

notes.model: claude-opus-5-5 through the Anthropic Messages API (llm.provider=anthropic), no fallback models, reviewer model = same model. Requests carry model, messages and max_tokens only (no tools, no thinking parameter); ARC's per-stage temperature is not sent because the model rejects it, so the API default applies.
notes.agent: ARC is not a tool-using coding agent: its 23-stage pipeline, its own code agent and its reviewers are prompt chains over plain chat completions. conditions.agent=claude means only that the provider is Anthropic; Claude Code is not involved. Generated experiments run as a plain subprocess in the container.
notes.effort: ARC has no effort setting; usage-log.patch sends output_config.effort='high' with every request. Haiku 5.5 thinks by default and ARC's per-stage max_tokens (for example 4096) is shared with the thinking tokens, so long outputs can still be cut short.
notes.venue: Not chosen by the system: export.target_conference=iclr_2026 comes from [systems.autoresearchclaw].
notes.tokens: ARC records no usage. A logging-only patch (usage-log.patch) appends each Messages API `usage` block to anthropic-usage.jsonl; cost is not computed. The same patch carries the RWE_OMIT_TEMPERATURE and RWE_EFFORT switches.
notes.time: No global wall-clock or budget cap in ARC; only the runner's limit applies. Per experiment run 3600 s, refinement iterations 10, repair cycles 3.
notes.input: Chinese pack text goes verbatim (candidate files concatenated, with <!-- file --> markers) into prompts.extra_prompts of 18 stages. ARC takes one topic string and checks generated code against it, so research.topic is the candidate TASK.md verbatim with whitespace collapsed. Literature queries come from the stage-3 model plan; ARC's ASCII keyword splitter and its whitespace-based query expansion yield a few useless queries from the Chinese text. Starter papers are guidance text only: ARC cannot ingest seed papers.
notes.search: Web search, crawling, GitHub, HF Hub, Gemini and OpenCode are off. Literature search in stage 4 uses ['openalex', 'semantic_scholar'] through ARC's own clients behind the shield proxy; stages 8, 17, 22 and 23 (novelty, citation verification) always also query arXiv, CrossRef and DataCite; the shield date-bounds those API calls like the others (a late DOI answers 403).
notes.server_side_search: Not reachable: every request to api.anthropic.com is built in researchclaw/llm/anthropic_adapter.py:136-148 and carries only model, messages, max_tokens, optional temperature, output_config.effort and system, never a tools or web_search field; the OpenAI-compatible client (OpenRouter :online / plugins) is not used (llm.provider=anthropic), web_search.enabled=false, Gemini is only used by the disabled figure_agent.nano_banana. Provider hosts are only tunnelled by the shield, so such a path would be invisible to the audit.
notes.secrets: Generated experiment code inherits the container environment, including the API keys (ARC offers no switch to scrub it).
notes.profile: project.profile=ml_generic is fixed for all tasks; research.domains is left empty because the literature screen rejects papers outside the stated domain (a theory task failed with domains=[machine-learning]).

preinstalled.zh: 上游锁定依赖（uv sync --frozen）加兼容补丁 compat.patch；TeX Live（含 fonts-extra、latexmk）；给 agent 用的研究 Python 环境 /opt/research
preinstalled.en: upstream's locked dependencies (uv sync --frozen) plus compat.patch; TeX Live (with fonts-extra and latexmk); a research Python environment for the agent in /opt/research

notes.agent: No external coding agent: EvoScientist runs its own in-process planner/research/code/debug/writing sub-agents (LangChain deepagents) on the one configured model. conditions.agent only selects the provider; Claude Code and Codex are not used.
notes.model: Main agent, sub-agents and EvoScientist's auxiliary calls (tool selector, memory workers, summariser, graders) all use the configured model; auxiliary_model and model_fallbacks are empty.
notes.effort: Upstream hard-wires effort=max and max_tokens=128000 for Anthropic models. compat.patch makes the effort come from EVOSCIENTIST_REASONING_EFFORT (= conditions.effort); max_tokens stays 128000 (a cap, not a cost driver). Adaptive thinking (display=summarized) is upstream and not switchable.
notes.paper: The core writes a Markdown report (final_report.md); the EvoSkills paper-writing skill gives a generic LaTeX `article` skeleton with no ICML/ICLR/NeurIPS style and no compile step. The image has TeX Live (latexmk, fonts-extra) but no venue style files; the task asks for an official template, so a venue-formatted PDF depends on the agent obtaining the style through the shield. No extra pipeline stage was added; absent items are listed in result.missing.
notes.tools: skill_manager (git clone of any repository as a skill) is not registered (compat.patch); the Tavily key is not set so tavily_search does not exist; LANGGRAPH_CLI_NO_ANALYTICS=1; EvoSkills is baked in at its pinned commit. The execute shell and the EvoSkills paper-navigator scripts reach the world only through the shield; S2_DATE_CUTOFF is not set (the shield bounds dates).
notes.server_side_search: Not reachable: EvoScientist binds no provider-side search tool to any model (its only tools are think_tool, tavily_search when TAVILY_API_KEY is set, MCP tools from mcp.yaml, deepagents built-ins and skills; EvoScientist/EvoScientist.py:671-672 and 754-755 at the pin; the one bind_tools call is the tool selector's own output schema, middleware/tool_selector.py:166). TAVILY_API_KEY is not passed and the image has no mcp.yaml, so no search tool exists. Anthropic/OpenAI hosts are only tunnelled by the shield, so a provider-side search would be invisible to the audit.
notes.credentials: The provider key is in the process environment and EvoScientist's execute shell inherits the environment (upstream has no switch); the key is therefore visible to the agent's shell. It is a run-scoped copy and is not logged by this adapter.
notes.memory: A fresh data dir per run (baked skills, empty memory). Memory workers, skill synthesis and the scheduler stay at upstream defaults, so their LLM calls count in the usage log.
notes.limits: async sub-agents off (README advice for scripted runs); recursion_limit=1000000; model retry wait in auto-mode 1800 s (time without progress counts as wall time); execute timeout 300 s per command. No token or cost budget exists.
